documents.title: Establishing Expectations: Syllabus Language and Policies for Generative AI Use
documents.stance_why: The page sets no rule itself: it says the examples 'are not official MSU policies' and offers four levels ('It's not allowed', 'allowed with appropriate attribution', 'allowed in limited instances', 'encouraged broadly or required') for each instructor to choose, so the stance is delegates with tiers.
documents.summary: Faculty-center page telling instructors to set AI expectations in each syllabus. It offers four use levels and three sample syllabus statements (allow, prohibit, require), stating these are not official MSU policy; it also covers co-creating expectations with students and citing AI.

units.why: Instructors are told they 'should set expectations' in the syllabus, class and assignments, so this is a syllabus-statement duty addressed to instructors at course start; P09 fits because it covers stating AI expectations in the syllabus.
units.anchor: Instructors should set expectations for students in the syllabus
units.frag_start: Instructors should set expectations
units.frag_end: generative AI can be used from the beginning.

units.why: The page offers four named levels of use as examples ('Four examples ... could be'), so naming tiers of use matches P05; it lists examples and grants no permission, so the modality is informs.
units.anchor: Four examples for content-generating AI could be:
units.frag_start: Four examples for content-generating AI
units.policy: The center offers four example levels of AI use for content-generating AI: not allowed, allowed with appropriate attribution, allowed in limited instances, and encouraged broadly or required.
units.resolution_why: A coded modality may, B coded informs. The source says only 'Four examples for content-generating AI could be:' followed by the levels, an illustrative list and not a grant of permission, so informs. Both gave P05, instructor, before-course. B's anchor alone does not state the four levels, so A's normalized policy is kept.

units.why: First tier: 'It's not allowed: Only content done by a student ... is accepted', a default ban option for an assignment (P01).
units.anchor: Only content done by a student or as part of an assigned group is accepted.
units.frag_start: It's not allowed: Only content
units.policy: Under the example level 'It's not allowed', only content done by a student or as part of an assigned group is accepted.

units.why: This tier allows AI-assisted work 'when students clearly identify what parts' were AI generated, so the core rule is disclosure with each submission (P24) rather than the permissive default P02.
units.anchor: allowed when students clearly identify what parts of the assignment were AI generated
units.frag_start: It's allowed with appropriate attribution
units.policy: AI-assisted work on some assignments is allowed when students clearly identify what parts of the assignment were AI generated and how it helped them.

units.why: This tier allows AI 'to prepare for assignments by brainstorming' with students showing how it helped; brainstorming (P15) is the specific permitted use, while the showing requirement is secondary.
units.anchor: AI can be used to prepare for assignments by brainstorming
units.frag_start: It's allowed in limited instances
units.policy: AI can be used to prepare for assignments by brainstorming, but students must show how it helped them reach the result.

units.why: Fourth tier: 'Use is encouraged broadly or required', an option where AI is welcomed or expected (P02).
units.anchor: Use is encouraged broadly or required: Students can use AI but must identify
units.frag_start: Use is encouraged broadly or required

units.why: The page states 'these are not official MSU policies' and are starting points for individual courses, so the university guidance leaves the rule to each instructor (P04).
units.anchor: these are not official MSU policies around generative AI use
units.frag_start: Please note these are not
units.policy: The example syllabus statements are not official MSU policies and are guides for faculty to create policies and expectations for their individual courses.

units.why: The example 'allowing' statement says 'you may utilize AI language models, including ChatGPT' for writing assignments, a prose-specific permission (P18).
units.anchor: you may utilize AI language models, including ChatGPT, as a resource
units.frag_start: In this course, you may utilize
units.policy: In this example course, students may utilize AI language models, including ChatGPT, as a resource to support their writing assignments.

units.why: The sample says AI is 'not a substitute for your critical thinking and creativity' and tells students to 'apply it as a supplement ... and not rely solely on its suggestions', so students stay the primary thinker (P32); it limits how far the permitted use may go, so the unit stance is restrict.
units.anchor: apply it as a supplement to your writing process and not rely solely
units.frag_start: While the AI language models can
units.policy: In the example allowing statement, AI is not a substitute for the student's critical thinking and creativity; students apply it as a supplement to their writing process and do not rely solely on its suggestions.
units.resolution_why: Same passage, type, actor, phase and modality from both coders. They differed on unit_stance: A permit, B restrict. The source does not grant the permission here (the previous sentence does); this sentence caps reliance on AI ('not rely solely'), which is a limit on permitted use, so restrict.

units.why: 'Ultimately, you are responsible for the content and quality' makes students own their submission (P29).
units.anchor: you are responsible for the content and quality of your written assignment
units.frag_start: Ultimately, you are responsible

units.why: The statement says students 'should critically evaluate ChatGPT outputs for accuracy, potential bias, and relevancy', a verification duty (P31).
units.anchor: you should critically evaluate ChatGPT outputs for accuracy, potential bias, and relevancy
units.frag_start: Therefore, you should critically

units.why: Sample says writing must remain 'original and properly attributed, including citing outputs'; this is a citation duty (P24).
units.anchor: ensure that your writing remains original and properly attributed, including citing outputs
units.frag_start: When utilizing AI language models, it is essential
units.policy: Students ensure their writing remains original and properly attributed, including citing outputs or text generated by ChatGPT.

units.why: The sample says 'I encourage you to use AI language models to enhance your writing skills', a welcoming default (P02).
units.anchor: I encourage you to use AI language models to enhance your writing
units.frag_start: I encourage you to use AI

units.why: Students with questions are told to 'discuss them with me', inviting questions to the instructor about AI use; P10 covers asking the instructor.
units.anchor: please discuss them with me.
units.frag_start: If you have any questions
units.policy: Students with questions or concerns about using AI language models for writing assignments discuss them with the instructor.

units.why: Example 'prohibiting' language: 'I have decided to prohibit the use of ChatGPT or similar tools during this course' is a course-wide default ban (P01).
units.anchor: I have decided to prohibit the use of ChatGPT or similar tools during this course.
units.frag_start: This class will strive to create
units.resolution_why: A coded phase course-start, B during-work; everything else agreed (P01, must-not, prohibit, student). The sentence 'I have decided to prohibit the use of ChatGPT or similar tools during this course' is a rule that binds the students' work for the whole course, not an announcement of expectations. I coded it during-work and used the same logic for the requirement statement below.

units.why: The ban sample justifies itself: 'relying on them for this course undermines the learning objectives', i.e. outsourcing practice defeats skill building (P41).
units.anchor: relying on them for this course undermines the learning objectives
units.frag_start: While ChatGPT and other language models
units.resolution_why: A coded the actor as instructor and phase course-start; B coded student and general. The sample is written in the instructor's voice to students ('I want you to develop your skills') and explains why the ban exists, a rationale rather than an act of communicating expectations, so student and general. Both gave P41 informs.

units.why: The ban 'applies to all aspects of the course, including assignments, exams, and any form of communication', so the point is the blanket scope of the default ban (P01) and not an exam rule (P22), which would apply only to exams.
units.anchor: this requirement applies to all aspects of the course, including assignments, exams
units.frag_start: It is important to note that this requirement
units.policy: In the example prohibition, the ban applies to all aspects of the course, including assignments, exams, and any form of communication related to the course content.
units.resolution_why: A coded P22, during-assessment; B coded P01, general. The passage extends the course-wide ban to 'all aspects of the course, including assignments, exams, and any form of communication', so it states the scope of the default ban. Exams are one item in a list, so P22 (no AI on exams) is too narrow; P01 and general scope.

units.why: 'Any use ... will be considered a violation student code of conduct' classifies unauthorized AI use as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: will be considered a violation student code of conduct
units.frag_start: Any use of AI language models

units.why: Example 'requiring' language: 'I have decided to make the use of ChatGPT a requirement throughout this course', which builds AI into the work (P02, require).
units.anchor: I have decided to make the use of ChatGPT a requirement throughout this course
units.frag_start: This course will encourage the use
units.resolution_why: A coded phase course-start, B during-work; the type, modality and stance agreed (P02, must, require). The sentence makes ChatGPT use a requirement throughout the course, a rule on the students' work, so during-work (same logic as the prohibition statement).

units.why: MSU 'seek[s] to empower you with the necessary skills to navigate and leverage these advancements effectively' is the sample's professional-skill rationale for requiring AI (P44); as a rationale it is neutral.
units.anchor: empower you with the necessary skills to navigate and leverage these advancements effectively
units.frag_start: we seek to empower you
units.resolution_why: A coded actor instructor, phase course-start, unit_stance neutral; B coded student, general, encourage. The sentence is a rationale addressed to students ('empower you'), so student and general. Rationales are coded neutral elsewhere in this file (e.g. the P41 unit), so neutral.

units.why: The required-use sample says AI 'will be an integral part of your learning process and will contribute to your overall evaluation', so AI is part of assessment; it extends P02.
units.anchor: will be an integral part of your learning process and will contribute
units.frag_start: Applying AI language models, including ChatGPT
units.policy: In the example requirement, applying AI language models, including ChatGPT, is an integral part of the learning process and contributes to the overall evaluation and assessment in the course.

units.why: The instructor says 'I will provide guidance, resources, and assistance to help you effectively utilize ChatGPT', so the course teaches AI use and the instructor commits to supporting it (P44); P17 does not fit because no tool is provided.
units.anchor: I will provide guidance, resources, and assistance
units.frag_start: I will provide guidance, resources, and assistance
units.frag_end: within the framework of this course.
units.policy: In the example requirement, the instructor will provide guidance, resources, and assistance to help students effectively utilize ChatGPT.
units.fit_note: Coder A coded this UNCOVERED: 'Instructor commits to support and guidance for students when AI use is required; no sanctioned tool is provided so P17 does not fit.' P44 covers teaching effective AI use but not the instructor's commitment to support students.
units.resolution_why: A coded UNCOVERED and modality should; B coded P44 and must. The passage says the instructor teaches and supports effective ChatGPT use in a course that requires it, which P44 ('courses teach or demonstrate AI use') covers, with the support commitment kept in fit_note. 'I will provide' is a stated commitment, so must.

units.why: The note 'These suggestions were generated by ChatGPT and edited by CFE staff' discloses AI-made materials and their human editing (P48).
units.anchor: These suggestions were generated by ChatGPT and edited by CFE staff
units.frag_start: These suggestions were generated by ChatGPT
units.resolution_why: Only coder B found this note. The source says 'These suggestions were generated by ChatGPT and edited by CFE staff', which discloses that the page's sample language is AI-made and human-edited, a statement about AI use in course materials (P48). Kept; it is a real statement in the text and not navigation.

units.why: The page suggests that the instructor 'partner with and engage students in an initial discussion around the responsible use of generative AI' so students have a say in the rules; this is co-creating the policy with students (P67).
units.anchor: engage students in an initial discussion around the responsible use of generative AI
units.frag_start: Another strategy that can establish
units.policy: Instructors can partner with and engage students in an initial discussion around the responsible use of generative AI, which promotes transparency and gives students some agency.
units.fit_note: Both coders coded this UNCOVERED before P67 existed. Coder A's note: 'Co-creating AI expectations with students through an initial class discussion.' Coder B's note: 'Instructors co-create AI-use expectations with students in an initial class discussion.' P67 now covers it.
units.resolution_why: Both coders marked UNCOVERED for the same passage with the same actor, phase and modality. The type list now has P67 'Co-create the AI policy with students', which this passage states directly (an initial class discussion in which students have agency over how AI is used), so P67.

units.why: The discussion is an opportunity to 'point out and discuss' AI's 'inaccurate information and/or biased content that students could be accountable for', a verify-output warning (P31).
units.anchor: inaccurate information and/or biased content that students could be accountable for

units.policy: The discussion can point out Open AI's limitations, including issues with inaccurate information and/or biased content that students could be accountable for.
units.fit_note: Instructor-led discussion of AI's limitations; near P66 but the content is the verify-output warning, so P31.
units.resolution_why: A coded modality informs, B coded should; type and actor agreed. The source says the discussion 'can be an opportunity to' do this, a description of what instructors can do and not an instruction, so informs.

units.why: The page cites a Boston University policy that 'requires students to show how and give credit to AI tools when they are used'; it reports another institution's disclosure rule as a model (P24), so the modality is informs.

units.resolution_why: A coded modality must, unit_stance permit; B coded informs, require. The sentence reports what the cited BU policy requires, so informs. A disclosure duty attached to allowed AI use is coded permit elsewhere in this file, so permit.

units.why: The cited BU policy sets 'expectations for how instructors will assess and possibly penalize merely reproducing AI output use by students', so reproducing AI output as one's work is not acceptable (P19); the penalty is not concrete enough for P37.

documents.unit: Montana University System, Commissioner of Higher Education
documents.title: Commissioner's Directive: Generative AI Adoption and Use
documents.stance_why: The directive directs campuses to 'adopt campus-level essential practices' and 'establish clear AI use expectations for instruction' without itself allowing or banning student AI use, so it hands the decision to campuses.
documents.summary: System commissioner's directive telling campuses to engage with eight core AI principles, adopt essential practices and set clear instruction expectations. It names no student-level rule and promises system resources and updates.

units.why: The directive says it 'establishes a shared framework for responsible AI use across the Montana University System' with principles and practices, an institution-level framework (P56).
units.anchor: establishes a shared framework for responsible AI use across the Montana University System
units.frag_start: That document establishes a shared framework
units.policy: The Montana University System directive states that the MUS AI Task Force Recommendations establish a shared framework for responsible AI use across the Montana University System, organized around core principles, system-level actions and campus-level essential practices.
units.resolution_why: Only coder B found this. The directive says the Task Force document 'establishes a shared framework for responsible AI use across the Montana University System', an institution-level framework statement (P56). Kept. B's anchor alone does not name the document, so I added a normalized policy.

units.why: The preamble names risks 'to data privacy and security, academic integrity, research reliability, and equity of access', framing purpose; chosen P56 since it lists several concerns rather than one rule.

units.policy: Campus CEOs and chief academic officers ensure that leadership, faculty governance bodies and administrative units review and discuss the eight MUS core principles for AI use.

units.why: The directive lists the eight principles including 'academic integrity' and 'restricted uses', defining the system principles (P56).

units.policy: The eight MUS core principles are data privacy and security; transparency and accountability; bias awareness and mitigation; human discretion; protection of intellectual property; academic integrity; restricted uses; and use of approved and non-approved tools.
units.resolution_why: Only coder A found this. The directive lists the eight core principles by name (including academic integrity and restricted uses), which defines the system framework (P56). Kept; B mentioned the principles only inside its policy for the engage-with-principles unit. Topic 'governance' is not in the topic codebook and was dropped.

notes: Reconciled from coders A and B. Only two documents were screened in: the Center for Faculty Excellence expectations page (explicitly not official MSU policy; it offers four tiers and sample syllabus language) and the Montana University System Commissioner's directive (April 9, 2026; system-level, sets no student rule). No school or computing-unit policy found; course layer deferred. The directive refers to the MUS AI Task Force Recommendations, which were not in the saved text. The CFE sample syllabus statements are coded as the page presents them (allow, prohibit and require examples), so their actors and modalities describe the example language. Coder notes: A: 'No school or computing-unit policy found; course layer deferred.' B: 'No school, computing or course documents screened in.' Types UNCOVERED in coder files now map to P67 (co-create with students), P76 (operations), P70 (AI-literacy resources for students and staff). Topics 'governance' (coder A) is not in the topic codebook and was dropped.
